item.title: Robert Pattinson Named as the Next James Bond
item.description:
After seven years of rumors, wish lists and wild guesses, Hollywood’s most feverishly followed casting search is over: Amazon MGM Studios has chosen Robert Pattinson to play James Bond.

Pattinson, the 40-year-old English actor, will become the seventh man to play 007 in the official 25-film series. Pattinson is known for blockbusters like “Twilight,” “The Batman” and, most recently, “The Odyssey.”

“To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement,” Pattinson said in a statement.

He succeeds Daniel Craig, who announced in 2019 that he would depart the role. Craig’s decision set off a frenzy of speculation among Bond enthusiasts, bookmakers and the British tabloids. Who could be trusted to step into the multibillion-dollar franchise? What kind of Bond would click with a new generation? Should Bond be Black? Or female?

At various points, the supposed candidates included Idris Elba, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Hardy, Regé-Jean Page, Tom Holland, Jacob Elordi and Theo James.

Pattinson was chosen over Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner. The five actors underwent screen tests in London in late October. The auditions involved stunts, dialogue and camera presence; they were overseen by Nina Gold, an Oscar-nominated (“Hamnet”) and Emmy-winning (“Game of Thrones”) casting director. Bond auditions can be revealing: Henry Cavill, who lost the role to Craig in the previous casting search, told Men’s Health in 2019 that he was asked to re-enact a scene in which Sean Connery’s Bond emerged from a bathroom in nothing but a towel.

James Bond is one of the most coveted — and unforgiving — roles in moviedom. When Craig was cast in 2005, taking over from Pierce Brosnan, detractors complained that he was too blond, too short and insufficiently suave. Carping fans have long been part of the Bond tradition, but the internet gave them a new megaphone. Craig’s “fleshy” ears and “potato” face were mocked on message boards. One group even created a protest website, CraigNotBond.com.

Craig went on to become one of the most celebrated Bonds, but playing a superspy with a license to kill took a physical toll. Over five films, he suffered injuries to his shoulder, calves, knee and ankle while shooting action sequences, at one point questioning whether he could continue.

The character also comes with a complicated cultural legacy, including what Helen Mirren has called his “profound sexism.” Nor is Bond’s appearance the only thing purists obsess over. Even minor adjustments to his martini order can be treated as grounds for an international incident: The product-placement Heineken he drank in “Skyfall” did not go down smoothly.

But this is no ordinary 007 handoff.

Amazon is attempting to reinvigorate a series that has been without a new movie since 2021, with the hiatus on track to become the longest in Bond history. In the franchise’s absence, a new generation of moviegoers has come of age with little attachment to the glamorous British spy, gravitating instead toward superheroes, horror movies and video game adaptations.

Amazon is also proceeding without the Broccoli family, whose expert stewardship of the franchise — over six decades — turned it into one of the most valuable properties in Hollywood history.

Amazon acquired a 50 percent stake in the Bond movies as part of its $8.5 billion purchase of MGM in 2022. Barbara Broccoli and her half brother, Michael G. Wilson, retained ownership of the rest — along with final say over creative decisions. In 2025, after years of behind-the-scenes tensions over Amazon’s ambitions to expand the Bond universe, the tech giant wrested creative control from Broccoli and Wilson.

Albert “Cubby” Broccoli, her father and his stepfather, first brought James Bond to the big screen with “Dr. No” in 1962. The official series has since generated nearly $7 billion in domestic ticket sales alone, after adjusting for inflation. Some longtime fans have worried that the films will become more corporate and American in style, losing their distinctly British character. With so much at stake, Amazon recruited Amy Pascal, the former Sony Pictures chairwoman who has become one of Hollywood’s most successful producers. David Heyman, the producing force behind all eight “Harry Potter” movies, is also helping to chart Bond’s future.

The 26th Bond film — not counting two made outside the official series, “Casino Royale” (1967) and “Never Say Never Again” (1983) — will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, whose credits include the Oscar-nominated “Dune” movies. Steven Knight, creator of the crime drama “Peaky Blinders,” is writing the screenplay. It’s an original story. “Casino Royale” in 2006 was the last Bond movie based substantially on an Ian Fleming novel. There are no more to adapt.

A release date has not been announced. Bond movies typically require six to seven months of filming alone, making a theatrical debut before 2028 unlikely.

Tess Felder contributed reporting from London.

item.title: United Halts Flights as It Addresses ‘Widespread System Outage’
item.description:
United Airlines reported a “widespread system outage” on Monday, grounding planes and stranding passengers even as the nation’s aviation system was recovering from the ground stoppage that paralyzed air traffic late last week.

The airline said in statement that it was “troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights.” There was “no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,” it said, referring to its regional network.

In a separate statement on social media, United said that “our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible.”

United did not immediately provide additional details about the outage, which was reported as federal officials were trying to get to the bottom of the nationwide ground stop that halted all air travel nationwide for hours on Friday.

It also comes ahead of the busy Thanksgiving travel period.

Airlines sometimes experience short-lived technical disruptions and can recover quickly if the problem is swiftly addressed. But a lengthy outage can become destabilizing as pilots and flight attendants reach legal working limits and delays and cancellations ripple throughout a carrier’s network.

This is a developing story.

Niraj Chokshi and Ryley Ober contributed reporting.

item.title: Pilots Kept Contact With Controllers During Nationwide Halt to Flights
item.description:
Pilots were able to maintain communications with air traffic controllers and airline dispatchers during the nationwide halt to most departing flights imposed by federal officials for nearly five hours on Friday.

A representative of the union that represents about 17,000 pilots at American Airlines said on Monday that it had received no reports of crews losing radio contact with controllers. Some pilots noticed radio static, but that isn’t uncommon, said Dennis Tajer, a spokesman for the union, the Allied Pilots Association.

Even so, the union said it supported the hourslong ground stop called by the Federal Aviation Administration, a part of the Department of Transportation.

“Just because the national shutdown happened without incident, let that not be the catalyst for doubting if the right call was made,” said Mr. Tajer, who is a Boeing 737 captain and was stranded near Newark Liberty International Airport on Friday night. “You just don’t know what would have happened had you said, ‘Well, let’s take a chance and see.’”

Southwest Airlines dispatchers, who help to plan and guide the carrier’s flights, also reported no disruption of direct communications or data before the ground stop was ordered.

“Dispatchers did not experience any loss of communication with our flight crews or F.A.A. control facilities, and our tools and data feeds did not show any signs of disruption,” said Kevin Thurston, the president of Transport Workers Union Local 550, the union that represents dispatchers and meteorologists at the airline.

The F.A.A. has said that the technical outage was intermittent and not a blackout, noting over the weekend that some radio frequencies and radar feeds remained reliable.

The agency said the problem began when data began flooding an agency telecommunications network. An initial investigation identified two possible sources: a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Ark. An investigation is ongoing.

“Throughout the disruption, certain radio frequencies and radar feeds remained operational, allowing air traffic controllers to maintain communication with and track aircraft,” the agency said in a statement.

Even if primary communications had gone dark, aircraft are equipped with backups. Pilots can use emergency frequencies to speak with nearby planes and ground facilities. Aviation professionals can also use other tools to communicate with dispatchers, including text-based systems.

“We have plenty of knives in our boot,” said Mr. Tajer. “It doesn’t mean we want to use them.”

item.title: Appeals Court Weighs Pentagon’s Media Restrictions
item.description:
A federal appeals court in Washington on Monday heard arguments in litigation about a set of media restrictions put in place by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, including a rule that all reporters who visit the Pentagon must be accompanied by an escort.

The New York Times had sued to overturn the policy on First Amendment grounds. The three-judge panel pressed both sides with tough questions.

Under Mr. Hegseth, the Defense Department has moved repeatedly to curtail journalists’ access to the military complex, often arguing that the restrictions are necessary to protect national security. Beginning in October 2025, the agency said it could strip reporters of their press passes for soliciting or publishing classified information and some unclassified information. Instead of complying with the rules, journalists from mainstream outlets surrendered their press credentials.

The Times sued over the initial policy in December 2025, arguing that the policy violated journalists’ First Amendment rights to gather newsworthy information without the prospect of punishment. In March, Judge Paul Friedman of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ruled in favor of The Times.

Days later, however, the Pentagon released a new set of rules, including the escort requirement. The Times challenged the revised policy in a second lawsuit, and, again, Judge Friedman ruled in its favor, scolding the Pentagon for “such a blatant attempt to circumvent a lawful order of the court.”

The Pentagon appealed both of the judge’s rulings.

At Monday’s hearing, the appeals court panel considered the escort requirement and other elements of the Pentagon’s revised media policies from March, which sought to clarify the October 2025 rules.

Judge Judith W. Rogers, a member of the panel who was nominated by President Bill Clinton, questioned the government’s approach to the Pentagon press corps.

“It’s as though you didn’t like violin music, so the orchestra leader said, ‘Get out of my orchestra.’” And then after the court ordered the violinist back to work, said Judge Rogers, “you tie his hands.”

The more “apt” analogy, argued Jack Starcher, who represented the Defense Department, is where “the violinist is put back in the orchestra in a different seat or in a seat that he considers less favorable to him.”

“He’s in the practice room,” quipped Judge Rogers.

Judge Patricia Millett, who was nominated by President Barack Obama, asked the government about a rule that said that the Pentagon could bar a reporter if it had “any doubt” about whether a journalist might pose a security risk. She said that standard would be hard to challenge.

Mr. Starcher said that it’s “hard to answer questions about what these provisions will actually look like in effect because these provisions have never been allowed to go into effect.”

“So they’re not clear,” responded Judge Millett.

Judge Millett also grilled Theodore J. Boutrous, a First Amendment lawyer representing The Times. Does the First Amendment, asked Judge Millett, really protect a reporter who goes into the Pentagon and seeks to pry classified information from an employee that the journalist knows is not authorized to share it?

“You’re saying the First Amendment allows you to do that?” asked the judge.

“I am saying that, your honor. That is our system,” responded Mr. Boutrous.

Judge Millett also asked whether The Times could demonstrate adverse consequences from the escort rule, which has been in place for several months. Mr. Boutrous responded that declarations from numerous journalists show that the Pentagon’s rules pose a “significant burden” on reporters.

The other judge on the panel is Karen LeCraft Henderson, a nominee of George H.W. Bush. It is unclear when the panel will issue a ruling in the case.

The Times’s suit is one of several pieces of litigation between media companies and the federal government or Mr. Trump in recent years. In September, CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued over their expulsion from the White House grounds; though they secured a judge’s order restoring their press credentials, they remain barred from rotations in the pool that covers President Trump in confined spaces.

The Associated Press, furthermore, sued the White House after it was barred from pool coverage. That case is also before the federal appeals court in Washington. Mr. Trump has sued major news outlets — including The Times, The Wall Street Journal and television news networks — over their coverage.

item.title: The Long Arm of Inflation Has Reached Our Feet
item.description:
Americans are paying more for sneakers, boots and high heels, another sign of how inflationary pressures have spread to nearly every aspect of consumer spending.

The war in Iran has driven up the price of oil, which has raised the price of gas, groceries and other goods transported by ship and truck. The surge in energy prices has affected the footwear industry too, as the some of the materials used to make shoes are synthetic byproducts of petroleum and thus more expensive.

Increased production costs combined with higher tariffs on products manufactured in Asia pushed shoe prices up 2.1 percent in the United States in October to their highest level, according to the latest Consumer Price Index data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The figure from the same period last year is missing because of a federal shutdown.

Still, there’s little sign that prices will fall soon. “We expect to see record footwear prices for the full year,” said Gary Raines, the chief economist of the Footwear Distributors and Retailers of America, a trade association. “That is strongly influenced by those average duties prepared on footwear that have been trending higher over the last year and a half.”

Historically, footwear price inflation has averaged 0.35 percent every six months from 2000 through June 2026. In the first half of this year, it rose 2.3 percent, the biggest semiannual jump since pandemic-related supply chain problems upended shoe production four years ago.

Shoe companies have worked to keep prices steady on their most popular items, such as Nike Air Force 1s and Crocs classic clogs, but have turned to incremental price increases on less vital products.

But even some of the most prominent shoe lines have increased prices. This year, Deckers Brands, the owner of Ugg, raised the price of its classic sheepskin boot 2.6 percent to $195 and said its Hoka running shoe brand would see some price increases this fall.

Footwear executives have said throughout the year that their businesses have been pinched by higher costs of materials such as leather and textiles. Andrew Rees, the chief executive of Crocs, said in April that its resin clogs, made from a proprietary foam, faced cost pressure as disruptions from the war in Iran sent oil prices skyrocketing.

Top executives from Adidas, Steve Madden and Birkenstock have each said that higher freight costs, brought on by those high oil prices, have affected their businesses.

Birkenstock said it had raised some prices as it pushed costs on to consumers. Ivica Krolo, the chief financial officer of Birkenstock, suggested on a conference call with analysts and investors in August that price-conscious shoppers traded down to the brand’s cheaper offerings.

“Our pricing decisions are made with the goal of passing through inflation and protecting gross margin,” Mr. Krolo said. “Something that we do very consistently.”

American consumers have kept spending this year even as they struggle with higher costs of living, but they are starting to pull back. In September, U.S. retail sales rose just 0.8 percent, down from a 1.3 percent gain in the previous month. Shoppers are expected to prioritize value in their purchases as retailers enter the crucial holiday season.

“The consumer keeps showing up,” Matt Priest, the chief executive of the Footwear Distributors group, said of the retail landscape. “But we don’t know how long that will last.”

Since President Trump returned to the White House, many of the world’s largest footwear brands, including Nike, Adidas, Skechers, Puma and Crocs, have pushed the administration to lower tariffs and alleviate pressure on their margins. In a letter sent to Mr. Trump last year, they said that the new tariffs presented an “existential threat” to the industry and asked him to consider an exemption.

The industry got a reprieve in February when the Supreme Court ruled that Mr. Trump was not authorized to unilaterally impose tariffs, but new duties under a different statute took effect in July.

The world’s largest shoe exporters are China, India, Vietnam, Indonesia and Bangladesh, and the United States has assigned each of these countries additional tariffs on top of duties already applied to footwear.

The Trump administration also left footwear out of its latest rounds of tariff exclusions, which have included categories such as wind turbines and commercial aircraft.

In July, the American Apparel and Footwear Association, an industry trade group with members that include Adidas and Steve Madden, sent a letter to the U.S. trade representative’s office that requested a list of footwear and other goods be considered for lower tariff treatment.

“Tariff relief broadly benefits U.S. workers in our industry,” Beth Hughes, the group’s vice president of trade and customs policy, wrote in the letter. “U.S. consumers stand to benefit since tariff costs ultimately make their way to the final consumer.”

item.title: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
item.description:
The Justice and Commerce Departments announced late Monday that they were pursuing a criminal investigation of Megaspeed, a Singapore company once led by a woman whom U.S. officials believe worked as a Chinese intelligence asset while having an affair with Nvidia’s chief executive.

The announcement appeared to be an effort to counter criticism that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was slow to investigate Megaspeed. It has become the most prominent example of companies that American authorities believe are skirting export rules on the powerful artificial intelligence chips made by Nvidia, the world’s leading manufacturer.

Nvidia exports have exposed a rift in the Trump administration between officials who believe American A.I. technology needs to be kept out of China for national security reasons and others who want a more hands-off approach to export controls.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a TV interview on Friday that his department had been pushing for months to add Megaspeed to a trade blacklist, but that the Commerce Department “holds the pen.”

“You will have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said.

That the Justice Department was included in the Monday night announcement appeared to add heft to the investigation’s importance and signaled to critics that administration officials did not intend to ignore the issue.

Megaspeed was created and led for a time by Alice Huang, who U.S. officials say was an asset for Chinese intelligence. The New York Times reported last year that she and Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, had a close relationship, and last week Mr. Huang admitted that he had been unfaithful to his wife with Ms. Huang.

Mr. Huang resigned from Nvidia last week following another revelation that he had had a relationship with a woman who worked for him. It was a stunning downfall for an executive who led a firm that for a time was the most valuable publicly traded company in the world.Megaspeed has said that it complies with all laws and that Ms. Huang currently has no role in the company. She has not returned requests for comment, and the Chinese government has dismissed the spying claims.

The Monday night news release confirming the criminal investigation was also unusual because officials do not typically discuss their inquiries until they are completed. The departments said that they would work together to “bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred.”

President Trump on Monday acknowledged that Mr. Bessent and Mr. Lutnick had been at odds over how hard to crack down on a loophole that has allowed China to access advanced A.I. chips through data centers in other countries.

“One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China,” Mr. Trump said of his two cabinet secretaries. “Both are acceptable, but they’re different views.”

The news release said that the Commerce Department had initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. In May 2025, the department requested records from Nvidia on its sales to Megaspeed. Commerce officials visited the company in June 2025 and interviewed Ms. Huang, it said.

The Justice Department then took the lead role in the Megaspeed criminal investigation, the news release said.

The New York Times reported last week that the Commerce Department investigation was halted last fall under atypical circumstances, after department investigators received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel seeking information about the inquiry.

Nvidia’s general counsel said that a top official at the department had given him permission to reach out about the case, alarming others in the department. The incident raised questions about what Commerce officials had discussed with Nvidia, and some viewed the interaction as potentially tainting the case. It was then transferred to the Justice Department.

The Commerce Department also said that Nvidia had placed Megaspeed on its “no-sell” list in June 2025.

But trade records obtained by The Times from ImportGenius, a data platform, show that Speedmatrix, a Megaspeed subsidiary in Malaysia, continued receiving large shipments of Nvidia technology for eight months after that.

Between October 2026 and February 2026, Speedmatrix received shipments of more than $800 million of export-controlled Nvidia A.I. technology, including Blackwell and H200 chips, which were banned from being sent to China.

Most of the Speedmatrix shipments went through third-party manufacturers that buy chips from Nvidia and make them into servers. But in February 2026, trade records show that Nvidia International Inc. sent a $13 million shipment of electronic equipment to Speedmatrix.

Nvidia provided a similar statement to The Times about the “block list” last week. It said that it received permission from the Commerce Department to ship some repair parts to Megaspeed after imposing its “block.”

Nvidia continues to list Megaspeed on its website as a cloud partner. Megaspeed advertised the relationship as recently as October, calling its Indonesian unit “a premier business partner of Nvidia.”

The Commerce Department said it had charged 17 defendants across six separate investigations over allegations of smuggling and sharply increased monetary penalties compared with those in the Biden administration.

Mr. Lutnick has clashed in recent months with other senior officials over rules that would clamp down on data centers in Southeast Asia that serve Chinese clients. The Commerce Department issued that rule Monday, but took the unusual step of saying that it had been “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council,” both agencies it had clashed with.

item.title: Fearing Chinese Rivals, U.S. Biotech Adopts a New Norm: Share Nothing
item.description:
It used to be that companies and scientists with ideas for new drugs couldn’t wait to announce their discoveries at meetings, in preprints and on their websites.

That is changing.

Researchers at the biotechnology firm Alnylam Pharmaceuticals have an unwritten policy: Do not reveal early-stage studies or discuss unpublished data, according to its founding chief executive, Dr. Christoph Westphal.

Jacob Becraft of Strand Therapeutics delays filing for patents to keep his company’s discoveries secret. And he is careful about disclosing his company’s intellectual property and confidential material, even to investors.

Alexis Borisy, a co-founder of Curie.Bio, which helps early-stage biotechs, says he tells scientists to “go dark” — don’t publish, don’t present posters at meetings, don’t even go to meetings.

The reason for this guarded stance? Fears that Chinese companies will seize on the biotechs’ discoveries and quickly beat them to market with the U.S. firms’ own inventions or with slightly altered versions that dilute market exclusivity.

“This is the world we’re in now,” Mr. Borisy said. Meetings are where scientists discuss new ideas. Publication is the lifeblood of science. But now, being too open too soon has become too risky, he and others said.

The concern is not only the risk of a significant economic hit if the United States cedes most of its biotech industry to China. It’s also a fear of direct effects on patients — the possibility that China might use access to drugs as a cudgel, experts said.

China has used its control of other resources that way, like its meting out of rare-earth minerals, a tactic used in trade wars with the United States. If China controls access to a valuable drug, like a cancer treatment for instance, it could use it for political leverage, warned the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology, an advisory group, in a report to Congress.

The Chinese Communist Party heavily subsidizes its biotech industry and says biotech is its highest priority, on par with artificial intelligence. Its five-year plan calls for China to make at least 25 percent of the world’s “first in class innovative medicines” over the next five years.

“With the trajectory they are on, I think they are being conservative,” said John Crowley, president and chief executive of BIO, an advocacy group. With lavish support, Chinese companies have been discovering more and more promising drugs. Mr. Crowley added that today about 30 to 35 percent of innovative medicines under development are of Chinese origin.

The United States, meanwhile, has a funding problem, said Cyriac Roeding, an investor. Small biotech companies depend on investors, which leaves them at the mercy of boom-and-bust cycles during the 10 to 12 years it takes to bring a drug to market.

The National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology made that same point in its report, writing that the nation needs a “‘private-public’ partnership for biotechnology driven by industry in collaboration with government.”

Multiple biotech executives, investors and those who study the industry, say their fears — that China is not playing fair, and that American biotech will lag in the future — are well-founded.

A recent paper in JAMA outlined China’s rise: In 2015, 48 percent of early-stage drug development was in the United States and 8 percent was in China. In 2024, 37 percent was in the United States and 32 percent was in China.

“My prediction is they will leapfrog us in biotechnology in the not too distant future,” said Dr. Steven Paul, a partner in the health care venture firm Third Rock Ventures.

Mr. Borisy cautioned that “disingenuous competition” was prompting American biotechs’ tactic of “going dark”: In one form of it, he said, Chinese investigators use A.I. agents that scour presentations at every scientific conference and rifle through every patent.

“The moment anything is out there, it is tracked,” Mr. Borisy said, adding that if there is a new idea, companies in China will seize on it. Many will get nowhere but, he said, if even a couple of these companies succeed, they can get a clinical trial going much faster than the U.S. inventors can.

Chinese companies, Mr. Crowley noted, can complete clinical trials “three times quicker than we can and at half the cost.”

Dr. Becraft said he and others had grown leery of representatives of Chinese companies at meetings who say they are investors and dangle promises of millions of dollars. These “investors,” he said, have sometimes turned out to be scouting for a company’s discoveries and do not in fact have money to offer. “I’ve stopped talking to them,” Dr. Becraft said.

At other times, Chinese competitors employ a technique that biotech firms call fast-follower/design-around: A U.S. company invents a drug and patents it; a Chinese company changes its design slightly to get around the U.S. patent.

That is what Revolution Medicines alleges happened to it. Its scientists worked for years to develop a drug for people with a gene mutation that drives nearly all pancreatic cancers. They patented the stunningly effective design, but then, seemingly out of nowhere, Chinese scientists licensed a nearly identical drug to a U.S.-based company, Erasca. Revolution Medicines said its trade secrets were “misappropriated.” Erasca denied the allegations.

Lisa Roessler says her company, Amyris, has been plagued by what she describes as outright data theft. Amyris engineers specialized yeast whose products can be used, for example, in vaccines and cosmetics. Its 15 commercial products took years and millions of dollars to develop. But recently, at trade shows, Chinese companies have been advertising the same products — presented with the same data, including the same number of people in clinical trials, the same results and other such impossibilities.

“One of the things we’ve seen is descriptions of our products, not just word for word but the data in brochures is literally our data, in the same format,” Ms. Roessler said.

China has denied previous claims that it steals trade secrets. “The Chinese government will not, in whatever form, engage in commercial theft or encourage or support such attempts by anyone,” said President Xi Jinping of China in a public speech in Seattle in 2015.

Stories of research appropriation abound, although few companies want to talk publicly about the details of what happened to them.

There’s a reason for that, said Melissa Roberts Chapman, president of KC Biohub. “If you were to make an allegation and later want to bring a drug to market in China, you might have trouble.”

Ms. Roessler added that most American companies depend on China to manufacture their drugs and conduct early-stage clinical trials. Those who criticize China can be, and have been, punished by denial of access.

Dr. Becraft said that after he began speaking out there was a five- to 10-fold increase in cyberattacks on his company’s computers and his private accounts. A U.S. government official told him it would be best if he did not travel to China.

The industrywide fear of reprisal was particularly apparent in May, when the U.S. International Trade Commission held a hearing in Washington on China’s threat to biotechs. The group had invited 297 individuals and groups to testify. But, Ms. Chapman said, when it came to the hearing, “only eight were in the room.”

Not everyone thinks the dangers are as real as they’re made out to be, however.

Peter Kolchinsky, an investor and managing partner of RA Capital Management, says that misguided fears about China are actually driving flawed policy proposals. “China hawks,” as he called them, often cite the rare-earth example, saying that just as China cornered the rare-earth market and used it for political advantage, it could do the same thing with drugs.

He disagreed. “Drugs are not commodities,” said Mr. Kolchinsky, whose more than 200 companies are mostly in the United States. “The equivalent of the rare-earth situation would be if the U.S. relied on China to manufacture all drugs.”

But, he added, that is not happening, and, with careful planning, it need not happen for individual drugs.

Mr. Kolchinsky said the solution to the China threat was not to restrict collaborations with or investment in Chinese firms. That can harm rather than help American companies, he said, because U. S. investors and companies will not know what’s going on in China. That will make it hard to know when a U.S. company’s product is the best.

What the ultimate path forward may be is unclear, however, when every avenue to presenting or sharing ideas could lead to theft. And few think legal actions will solve the bigger problem.

Today’s situation “is not an accident,” said Caitlin Frazer, executive director of the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology. Instead, it is the product of 20 or 25 years of a deliberate strategy by the Chinese government, with a doubling down on the effort in the latest update to the Chinese government’s five-year plan.

Last year, the commission published a report on how to save the nation’s biotech industry. It made 49 recommendations and said the United States needed to provide incentives for research, speed clinical trials and reduce investment risk.

Mr. Crowley of Bio said it was not too late for U.S. biotech. “Unlike in chips, where we totally lost it, we still have the lead in biotech,” he said.

But, he said, there is no time to waste: “We need to be sure we don’t wake up and see biotech wither.”

item.title: Texas Republicans Gave Elon Musk $1.7 Billion, Secrecy and Access. Now What?
item.description:
On Valentine’s Day in 2024, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott interrupted a private dinner with his wife to take a call from Elon Musk.

Mr. Musk had recently been rebuked by a court in Delaware, where his two largest companies, SpaceX and Tesla, were incorporated. A judge had voided Mr. Musk’s pay package at Tesla, valued at about $50 billion, calling it “an unfathomable sum.”

Mr. Musk had spent years building a close relationship with the Republican governor. Now, on the call, Mr. Musk wanted to know if Mr. Abbott would support Mr. Musk’s businesses if he incorporated them in Texas, rather than Delaware.

“One hundred percent,” Mr. Abbott said, recounting the story in a 2025 speech at the University of Texas School of Law.

Mr. Musk followed through, further entwining his trillion-dollar electric vehicle maker, Tesla, and his two-trillion-dollar rocket maker, SpaceX, with the state. Mr. Musk had been cultivating Texas’s Republican leaders since he moved there in 2020. For a while, the strategy paid off handsomely. Mr. Abbott held up his end of the Valentine’s Day bargain, awarding Mr. Musk and his businesses at least $1.7 billion in grants, tax breaks and other incentives in the past two years, according to a New York Times analysis.

Since this month’s election, Mr. Musk’s big bet on Texas has become vulnerable. Texans voted out many of his political allies, including Mr. Abbott, even after Mr. Musk gave Republicans nearly $500 million nationwide.

But unlike his breakup with California six years ago, Mr. Musk, 55, cannot easily pick up and leave this time. He is far more embedded in Texas than he ever was on the West Coast, where he started his business empire.

Tesla and SpaceX control seven major facilities in Texas that span at least 20,000 acres, including a spaceport and a lithium refinery, as well as a 100-million-square-foot semiconductor facility that is under construction. Mr. Musk personally owns 1,000 more acres in the state. By one estimate, his companies employ more than 20,000 people in the state. And Mr. Musk has formed more than 90 private companies in Texas and bought multiple properties. He even started his own city, called Starbase.

Mr. Musk has become “omnipresent” across the state, said Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University in Houston.

That means that for the foreseeable future, Mr. Musk may have to work with Texas Democrats, many of whom were elected after excoriating him on the campaign trail. James Talarico, the Democratic senator-elect, for one, said after the election that he did not intend to do Mr. Musk’s bidding.

Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa also took aim at Mr. Musk. In her first news conference as governor-elect, she announced that Mr. Musk’s attempts to buy a portion of a state park in South Texas near his rocket launch site — and her hometown — had been paused. In an interview with The Times, she took a more conciliatory approach, saying she welcomes Mr. Musk “but it needs to be about what a relationship can provide for Texas.”

Mr. Musk and his companies did not respond to requests for comment. SpaceX’s and Tesla’s shares fell after the election. Mr. Musk said earlier this month on X that those two companies “have prospered in Texas, because we were not constantly operating under an oppressive and extractive state government."

Mr. Musk moved to California in the late 1990s, about a decade after leaving his home country, South Africa. In the early 2000s, he started SpaceX in Los Angeles and took over Tesla, opening a factory in Fremont.

But after pandemic restrictions in 2020 led to a fight with local officials, Mr. Musk told The Wall Street Journal that December that the state had become complacent with business competition and that Silicon Valley was stifling start-up creation, so he was leaving for Texas.

Mr. Musk and his advisers at SpaceX and Tesla immediately began building relationships with the state’s Republican lawmakers.

SpaceX hired Jeff Miller, a strategist who worked with former Republican Speaker of the House Kevin McCarthy, to help Mr. Musk make inroads across the state. Since 2020, SpaceX has paid Mr. Miller’s firm, Miller Strategies, more than $1 million, according to lobbying records. Tesla and SpaceX together use 10 more individual lobbyists in Texas, according to state lobbyist registrations disclosed this year.

Mr. Musk also developed a rapport with Mr. Abbott, who has led the state since 2015. In 2021, Mr. Abbott said in a CNBC interview that he spoke with the billionaire frequently.

“Elon consistently tells me that he likes the social policies in the State of Texas,” Mr. Abbott said.

Mr. Abbott approved a slew of incentives for Mr. Musk’s businesses. Last year, Mr. Abbott awarded SpaceX a $17.3 million grant for the expansion of its Starlink satellite-internet service facility in Bastrop County, just outside Austin. Mr. Musk has other operations in the county, including for his tunneling venture, the Boring Company, a company town called Snailbrook, and more than two dozen acres where he had planned to start a school system.

“We love Texas,” Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX’s president, said in a statement at the time.

Mr. Abbott was also instrumental in greenlighting incentives for Mr. Musk’s mammoth semiconductor factory, known as Terafab, in Grimes County. The governor’s office announced a $30 million grant for the project in August, and has approved tax breaks estimated at more than $1.6 billion.

“Economic development incentives in Texas go through a rigorous statutory process with built-in review and accountability,” a spokesman for Mr. Abbott said.

Mr. Musk and his companies enjoyed a string of wins in the Texas legislature in recent years when Republicans led both legislative chambers, a streak that is now in doubt.

After lobbying by SpaceX, Texas lawmakers voted last year to add spaceports like Starbase, the company’s rocket launch site in South Texas, to the state’s “critical infrastructure” facilities. A separate bill made it illegal to fly drones over Starbase and other sites like it.

SpaceX also won greater control over closing Boca Chica Beach near Starbase for rocket launches, despite the fact that the Texas Constitution protects access to public beaches. In a related lawsuit that went to the state Supreme Court involving the beach, Ken Paxton, the outgoing Republican attorney general and an ally of Mr. Musk’s, intervened in the court case to support SpaceX, and later cheered the ruling.

It’s “exactly what’s needed to ensure SpaceX has a safe and operational launch site,” Mr. Paxton posted on X. Mr. Musk spent more than $200 million trying to get Mr. Paxton elected to the U.S. Senate. He lost to Mr. Talarico. Mr. Paxton’s office didn’t return a request for comment.

While Republicans still control the State Senate, Democrats won control of the Texas House in the midterms. At minimum, that will create gridlock for any measure that Mr. Musk and his companies try to pass, said Mr. Jones, the political science professor.

“He can’t expect the same preferential, sympathetic treatment from state government,” Mr. Jones said.

Mr. Musk has tried to keep many details of his expansion across Texas a secret, aided by the state’s business-friendly records laws and Mr. Paxton, who enforces them.

In Texas, a business can weigh in on public records disputes and ask the attorney general to keep the information from the public. Now Mr. Paxton is being replaced by Nathan Johnson, a Democratic state senator who has vowed to investigate whether SpaceX has improperly received grants from the state.

Last year, The Texas Newsroom, a collaboration of public radio stations, requested communications between Mr. Musk and his businesses and anyone working for Mr. Abbott in an effort to understand their relationship. Mr. Abbott’s office argued the records should not be released because they would reveal policy decisions, including details of how the state entices companies to invest, according to responses to the requests reviewed by The Times.

The office noted the records could include “intimate and embarrassing” details about Mr. Abbott and Mr. Musk and his companies. SpaceX’s lawyer asked Mr. Paxton to withhold the communications; his office ruled that many of the documents could be withheld.

Mr. Abbott eventually released about 1,400 pages of records. All but about 200 were redacted.

Last month, Ms. Hinojosa sued Mr. Abbott in Travis County District Court for access to the emails, accusing him of breaking a state law that allows legislative representatives to view confidential records. She detailed the closeness of the two men, including Mr. Musk’s Valentine’s Day call, first reported by The Texas Tribune.

The Texas court agreed with her and ordered the records be released. Mr. Abbott, who has called the legal action “a sham lawsuit,” appealed the decision. A court ruled in his favor, blocking Ms. Hinojosa’s access to the records.

As she prepares to take office, Mr. Musk is still awaiting approval for an undisclosed amount of incentives on at least two major projects: a planned data center near its Starbase headquarters and a solar cell manufacturing plant that Tesla is building in Fort Bend County known as Project Crystal Sun.

Over the summer, officials representing Tesla asked the state for property tax breaks. They offered a hint at how they might respond to stronger resistance from Democrats: Without those incentives, “Tesla would be forced to further evaluate this potential investment outside of the state of Texas,” they said, according to state documents.

item.title: As Trump and Xi Mingle, Their Governments Are Arming Up
item.description:
In front of the cameras, President Trump and China’s Xi Jinping have showcased a budding friendship, cemented by state visits, friendly pats on the arm and the occasional shared laugh.

But the public cordiality masks a different reality. Their governments are hardening their economic defenses and putting up new barriers to trade and investment. It has become more difficult for the two countries to invest, trade or do business with each other.

More good will is expected when Mr. Trump arrives in the Chinese city of Shenzhen this week for his third meeting with Mr. Xi this year. Yet the divide between their governments is becoming harder to ignore. Each meeting has been preceded by fresh economic offensives that are driving the world’s two largest economies further apart.

Shortly before Mr. Trump was scheduled to land in Asia, his administration moved to restrict China’s access to advanced artificial intelligence chips through data centers outside its borders, proposing a new rule to close a loophole that experts said would further inflame tensions. On Tuesday, China called the rule a “textbook case of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction” that “disrupts the stability of global industrial and supply chains.”

It was the latest in a series of moves from both China and the United States in recent weeks to label new sectors of their economies off limits in the name of national security. Beijing has designated more technologies as strategically vital, placing tighter controls on their export. Washington has proposed barring American investment in Chinese biotechnology, hypersonic weapons and artificial intelligence.

The confrontation has spilled beyond their two countries’ borders into global supply chains. China is building a fortress around technologies and critical materials on which much of the world depends, forcing other countries and multinational companies to contend with the fallout.

“There are more barriers than bridges being built,” said Ben Kostrzewa, a partner at the law firm Hogan Lovells in Hong Kong. “Each of these moves on its own is another brick in the wall and it is becoming harder and harder to invest in the other country.”

The steady buildup of those barriers began nearly a decade ago as a tit-for-tat tariff war during Mr. Trump’s first term. It has evolved into a far broader showdown for economic and technological supremacy.

China, in particular, has shifted its tactics. Once largely content to answer American tariffs and sanctions with reciprocal measures that were often symbolic, Beijing is now going on the offensive. It is wielding its dominance in manufacturing and critical supply chains to remind Washington — and the rest of the world — of the costs of confronting it.

The rivalry reached a low point last year, when both sides imposed tariffs so steep they amounted to a de facto trade embargo. China then threatened to tighten its controls on rare earths, the essential materials used in everything from smartphones and electric vehicles to fighter jets.

In October 2025, Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi eased tensions by agreeing to a truce and reciprocal state visits.

The two visits this year were heavy on ceremony. When Mr. Trump traveled to Beijing in May, he was greeted by military bands and cheering children. When Mr. Xi landed in Maryland in September, he was welcomed on the tarmac by Mr. Trump. There have been raised glasses, shared walks and moments of banter.

After Mr. Xi’s visit two months ago, the two governments agreed to extend their yearlong truce and reduce tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods. Yet neither side formally confirmed the extension until hours before the agreement was set to expire, just a week before Mr. Trump’s planned arrival in China.

Even then, the reprieve was limited. The renewed truce, which suspended certain tariffs and export controls, runs only through January.

And despite Beijing’s pledge to ease restrictions on exports of rare-earth metals and other critical minerals, some American companies still struggle to obtain supplies, said Erin Browne, the U.S. Treasury Department’s under secretary for international affairs.

“We’re making sure that we’re getting equal treatment across companies, across sectors, but also across materials or rare earths,” Ms. Browne said. “The strength of the relationship between our two presidents goes a long way in helping to move that along.”

Yet the personal rapport has done little to restrain an emboldened China, which has signaled it is no longer afraid of escalating economic warfare.

Beijing has strengthened its arsenal of countermeasures against American blacklists of its companies. It has created new legal mechanisms to block foreign sanctions, and Chinese companies have brought legal actions against foreign businesses, including JPMorgan Chase and Citibank, in Chinese courts for complying with American restrictions.

This year, Beijing introduced sweeping rules empowering regulators to inspect corporate records and prevent executives from leaving China if their companies are found to be helping to shift supply chains out of the country.

It has also established a national security review system for foreign investments, using it to block Meta’s $2 billion acquisition of Manus and SoftBank’s $5.4 billion takeover of ABB Robotics.

Together, these developments reflect “a very prominent change” in China’s approach, said Zhao Minghao, a professor at Fudan University. Beijing is assembling legal and regulatory tools built around economic and technological security, he said, and “exploring using actual cases to give these laws ‘teeth,’ so that they can truly be implemented and put to use.”

Its new strategy aims to protect control over the technologies and industries that give it a competitive edge.

Beijing has recently started restricting exports of dozens of technologies related to artificial intelligence, biotechnology and solar power. Under the rules, Chinese companies need government approval before transferring or sharing the covered technologies overseas.

For its part, Washington is seeking to cut off the capital that helps finance China’s technological ambitions. A Treasury Department proposal to expand those investment limits could make investing in broad swaths of China’s technology sector nearly impossible.

“We’re in the early stages of financial decoupling,” said H.K. Park, managing director and national security expert at Crumpton Global.

Analysts in both countries see little prospect of reversing the ever-wider restrictions on trade, technology and capital.

That leaves Mr. Xi and Mr. Trump with a shrinking set of issues on which they can strike deals. When the two leaders meet in Shenzhen, they may find room to bargain over tariffs. But the technologies, investments and critical materials at the heart of their rivalry are becoming harder to negotiate.

“Tariffs are a minor issue,” said Zhou Yong, a partner at the JunHe Law Offices in Beijing. They are among the few areas where both governments can still reach agreement.

“The real sticking points are competition in A.I., high tech, and chips, and China’s export curbs on rare earths,” he said.

“These are higher-stakes bargaining chips that both sides feel difficult to negotiate now.”

item.title: Disney Plans to Finance Growth With $3 Billion in Cost Savings
item.description:
Disney’s long-dead stock price has climbed 19 percent since Josh D’Amaro took over as chief executive in March. On Tuesday, he gave Wall Street a glimpse of how he plans to keep it going.

To drive growth, Disney said it would cut $3 billion in annual operating costs by 2029, with most of the savings earmarked for reinvestment in its businesses. Spending on content will increase 9 percent in the coming year, for instance, to $26 billion. The marketing budget for streaming will also rise. Disney also said it would triple its original programming in overseas markets over the next three years, citing the importance of locally produced content in attracting and engaging Disney+ subscribers.

Upgrading technology and expanding the use of artificial intelligence are also priorities. Disney announced, for instance, that it had started testing an A.I. tool — developed with Google — to simplify planning and booking vacations at Walt Disney World. Disney+ will add podcasts and more live sports. Videos from TikTok creators will arrive on the service next month.

How will Disney achieve the savings? The company didn’t say. But deep job cuts are expected early next year.

Mr. D’Amaro made the announcements as part of an upbeat fourth-quarter earnings report. In a surprise, however, Disney said it would stop disclosing operating profit for its entertainment streaming business. Netflix, Disney and Warner Bros. Discovery all stopped reporting subscriber totals in recent years. But most of Disney’s biggest rivals, including Netflix, NBCUniversal and Paramount Skydance, continue to provide detailed financial information about streaming profitability.

Disney is making the change after reaching a double-digit annual profit margin for streaming, a yearslong goal. The margin was nearly 12 percent.

Disney justified the decision by saying it was focused on the financial performance of its entertainment division as a whole — how much income it generates from its movies and television shows across streaming, traditional television, the box office, third-party licensing and consumer products. (A less charitable reading: Disney is reducing scrutiny of streaming margins just as increased spending could put pressure on them.)

For the quarter that ended on Oct. 3, Disney had revenue of $25.95 billion, a 16 percent increase compared with a year earlier. Adjusted per-share profit increased 59 percent, to $1.77. Both results beat analyst expectations.

Disney benefited from an extra week in its fiscal calendar; improved streaming profitability; a bump in merchandise licensing revenue ahead of “Avengers: Doomsday,” which arrives next month; and strong ticket sales for “Toy Story 5.” ESPN was bolstered by strong advertising sales and Disney’s acquisition of the NFL Network. Disney’s theme park and cruise businesses delivered $1.6 billion in operating profit, a 23 percent increase compared with a year earlier.

Disney also said it would increase its annual dividend by 33 percent, to $2 a share, and spend another $9 billion on stock buybacks in the coming year.

item.title: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
item.description:
The Trump administration’s proposal to restrict China’s access to advanced A.I. chips overseas rattled Southeast Asia on Tuesday, threatening a data center investment boom fueled by Chinese companies using the region to sidestep U.S. restrictions on Nvidia’s most powerful chips.

Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Singapore have become offshore computing hubs for Chinese companies such as Alibaba and ByteDance. Data center operators in those countries provide the Chinese firms with remote access to advanced Nvidia chips they cannot buy directly or bring into China.

The strategy has drawn billions of dollars in investment to the region. But in Washington, officials seeking tighter controls on China’s A.I. sector have increasingly viewed data centers as a workaround that poses economic and national security risks.

Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was ousted last week after revelations he had an affair with a woman who formed a Singaporean data center company called Megaspeed. U.S. authorities deemed the woman, Alice Huang, to be an asset for Chinese intelligence services, and they are investigating Megaspeed over allegations of smuggling chips to China. China has denied that Ms. Huang was spying for it.

Separately, Nvidia’s board of directors announced on Tuesday that it had established a committee to oversee “the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.” Nvidia’s board is engaged in a search for a permanent successor to Mr. Huang. The company’s interim chief executive, Colette Kress, is set to preside over the release of the company’s latest quarterly financial results later on Tuesday.

Shares of technology companies tumbled on Tuesday. In trading in Hong Kong, Alibaba fell 5 percent, while Tencent’s stock dropped nearly 4 percent. The Chinese A.I. firms MiniMax Group fell 7 percent and Z.AI Co. declined 5 percent. In the United States, tech stocks mostly stabilized from a sell-off that day before. Nvidia shares were up slightly ahead of the start of regular trading in New York.

Governments across Southeast Asia were scrambling to assess the administration’s 132-page policy, released by the Commerce Department on Monday, as President Trump traveled to Asia for diplomatic meetings.

The timing illustrated how A.I. has moved to the center of global diplomacy. Mr. Trump was expected to meet leaders of several affected countries at the ASEAN summit of 11 Southeast Asian nations in Manila. Then, he traveled to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation, or APEC, forum.

The rules, which take effect in 90 days, will require overseas data center operators to obtain a license from the United States government before supplying a “significant volume” of computing power to companies based in countries deemed high-risk, including China, Iran and Russia.

Licenses would also be required to export advanced chips to companies headquartered in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia or Brazil, countries the Trump administration identified as posing a heightened smuggling risk.

The Singaporean government said in a statement on Tuesday that it was investigating Megaspeed and was “engaging the relevant U.S. authorities on the scope and implementation of the measure.”

“As a global hub for technology and trade, Singapore will continue to safeguard the integrity of our business environment and continued access to advanced semiconductors and computing capabilities for legitimate companies operating here, and act against those who flout our laws,” the statement read.

Indonesia said it was seeking industry input and pledged to enforce American export controls. The government is developing a trade framework to “facilitate legitimate trade” while preventing sensitive technologies from being “diverted or misused,” the country’s Government Communication Agency said.

Steve Okun, chief executive of APAC Advisors, a geopolitical consulting firm, said countries such as Malaysia had benefited from maintaining close ties with Washington and Beijing. The new restrictions could make that balancing act harder to sustain.

“The ‘don’t make us choose’ era is coming to an end,” he said. “When it comes to A.I. and sensitive technologies, countries will need to choose the U.S.-led tech stack versus China.”

Ong Kian Ming, Malaysia’s former deputy minister for investment, trade and industry, said he hoped the Trump administration, which has been divided over A.I. chip export restrictions, would revise the rules before they take effect.

Otherwise, he said, the restrictions could create an opening for Chinese companies to offer competing chips. “This may mitigate some of the negative impact of not allowing these players to access Nvidia GPU chips,” he said.

Xinyun Wu contributed reporting.

item.title: Kalshi’s Warning Against Insider Trading, Courtesy of Martha Stewart
item.description:
There Martha Stewart is, in an uncanny recreation of her 1990s television show, baking a pecan pie. But while she preps the crust, the camera turns to a spice shaker labeled “confidential information.”

“We won’t be using that ingredient,” she says, warning, “If you have information that hasn’t been made public, you don’t trade. Simple.”

The skit wasn’t from “Saturday Night Live.” It’s an ad from Kalshi, a prediction market.

It’s the latest effort by Kalshi to promote itself as a by-the-rules platform for betting on real-world events like sports and elections — and not one where insiders can profit by taking advantage of the masses. And it comes as the company announces new policies that it says makes its insider trading surveillance policies more effective.

“At the end of the day, people want to put their money somewhere safe and regulated,” Luana Lopes Lara, a founder and the chief operating officer of Kalshi, said in an interview.

Of the ad, she said, “We needed to make something that would be kind of very exciting and have a virality component.”

Insider trading remains a sore subject for Kalshi and its chief rival, Polymarket, especially after high-profile accusations against a U.S. soldier involved in a mission to capture Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela, the former politician George Santos and a Google software engineer.

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have raised concerns about insider trading, especially when it comes to sensitive markets like elections. A candidate who bets on his own race “undermines the overall integrity of the American electoral process,” Senator Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts, and Senator John Curtis, Republican of Utah, wrote to the chief executives of Kalshi and Polymarket last month.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which oversees the industry, has already warned platforms to limit so-called mention markets, in which traders bet on whether someone will say a particular word during an event like a corporate earnings call.

Both prediction market operators say that insider trading violates their policies, and that they regularly investigate instances of potential impropriety. They refer suspected cases to the C.F.T.C.: Kalshi has made more than 50 referrals to law enforcement in the second and third quarters of this year alone, according to the company.

As Kalshi prepares to run the Stewart campaign — aided after Ms. Stewart and Ms. Lopes Lara met this summer at the World Cup final — the company will announce on Tuesday that it will adopt recommendations from an independent group of market integrity experts that the company says will further refine its insider trading surveillance.

In essence, the company is lowering oversight on the majority of markets where insider trading is unlikely, representing 98 percent of trading volume. But it is also adopting greater scrutiny for markets where illicit trading might be more prevalent, such as betting on the introduction of a new cryptocurrency token.

“If you’re not willing to innovate,” said Robert DeNault, Kalshi’s head of enforcement, “you’re going to get a flood of alerts.”

Self-policing, in the form of referrals to federal authorities, is just one part of cracking down on insider trading in prediction markets, said Karen Woody, a professor of law at Washington and Lee University’s School of Law. The case law involving such prosecutions is still evolving, with the defendants in the Google and Maduro cases trying novel legal defenses.

And the C.F.T.C. itself remains limited in its resources: “It already has a lot on its plate,” Ms. Woody said.

Policing insider trading on these platforms is getting more complicated, especially as they open newer and potentially more volatile markets such as so-called perpetual futures for individual stocks, which resemble 24-hour stock trading.

Mr. DeNault has said he expects to continue growing Kalshi’s surveillance team, which already doubled over the past year, and that prediction markets will cooperate more with each other to guard against insider trading.

“We’ll probably continue to scale up,” he said.

item.title: Nvidia’s High-Stakes Moment
item.description:
Andrew here. We’re getting ready for our annual DealBook Summit on Wednesday. The past week has brought an avalanche of news, and you’ve sent us some extraordinary questions for our onstage interviewees, including Vice President JD Vance, Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada, Elon Musk of SpaceX, Sam Altman of OpenAI, Christine Lagarde of the European Central Bank, Satya Nadella of Microsoft, the entrepreneur Hailey Bieber and many more.

We’ll have a special edition of DealBook tomorrow morning with information about how you can follow along all day. Now onto today’s news.

Stock markets appear poised for more losses as the artificial intelligence sector, and Nvidia in particular, continued to weigh on investors.

The chipmaker is facing its latest crucible since the resignation last week of its leader, Jensen Huang: quarterly earnings. They will underscore the debut of Colette Kress’s era as interim C.E.O., with analysts ready to pepper her with questions about the health and future of the chipmaker, including whether her old boss might seek a comeback and whether she’ll turn off the investment spigot.

The latest:

Nvidia shares are up in premarket trading. The company’s stock has declined 27 percent since late October, wiping out over $1 trillion in market value.

Nvidia’s performance last quarter isn’t what investors are worried about. Analysts expect the company, whose chips power most of the A.I. boom, to have nearly doubled revenue, to $109 billion.

Analysts want to know what lies ahead for Nvidia. That includes the true state of its China business amid questions about Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an executive at a data center company accused of smuggling Nvidia chips to China and who U.S. intelligence agencies believe was a Chinese asset. (On Monday, the Trump administration moved to block China from gaining access to Nvidia chips via data centers based outside its borders.)

They will also want to know about efforts to find a permanent replacement for Huang, particularly as a “who’s who” list of Silicon Valley seeks to restore the former Nvidia chief to his position. Also potentially in favor of such a move: President Trump, who told reporters on Monday, “I would not mind that.”

Nvidia’s board isn’t considering bringing Huang back as C.E.O., DealBook hears. That said, the three leading candidates for the job, based on trading on Kalshi, are Rene Haas, the C.E.O. of the chip designer Arm; Ian Buck, a top technical executive at Nvidia; and Huang himself.

Some analysts may also ask about the solidity of Nvidia’s chip sales after Huang’s departure, particularly after Elon Musk, a major customer, warned publicly that “at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”

All eyes will be on Kress, Nvidia’s former C.F.O., who, news reports suggest, had raised questions about the company’s increasingly expansive financial guarantees to A.I. businesses.

One challenge that may emerge for her is Huang’s two children, Madison Huang and Spencer Huang, and his son-in-law, Nico Caprez, all of whom remain executives at the company. The Times reports that Kress — and many other executives — had clashed with Madison Huang, who essentially served as her father’s chief of staff.

Deutsche Bank documents reveal that the lender leaked President Trump’s tax filings in 2017. Whistleblowers disclosed that nugget, according to The Financial Times, in a dump of more than 15 million internal documents, which included new details about the German lender’s ties to Trump, the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein and Russian oligarchs. Shares in the bank fell sharply on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange on Tuesday over concerns that the bank and its C.E.O., Christian Sewing, could face international political pressure over the leaks.

Tech glitches hobble banks and flights. JPMorgan Chase said operations had returned to normal after a software bug blocked thousands of customers from accessing their online accounts at big U.S. banks and Zelle, the money transfer service. Elsewhere, what United Airlines described as a “widespread system outage” grounded its planes for about an hour on Monday, further fraying travelers’ nerves after a nationwide ground stop that canceled at least 20,000 flights.

A big delivery platform merger reportedly faces antitrust scrutiny. The Justice Department is set to review DoorDash’s planned roughly $17 billion takeover of Instacart, the grocery delivery app, Reuters reports, citing unnamed sources. The combination of DoorDash, the largest U.S. delivery service, with Instacart comes as competition intensifies in the sector. DoorDash will pay Instacart a $1.25 billion breakup fee if the deal fails antitrust review.

California sues OpenAI over artificial intelligence agents that went rogue. The state’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, filed a lawsuit accusing the company of putting the public at risk by failing to put appropriate safeguards on its A.I. after OpenAI agents were involved in several incidents, including a hack attack of the platform Hugging Face. California’s move comes as states vie with the Trump administration for greater oversight of the technology.

For years, Martha Stewart spoke relatively little about her conviction over lying about a stock trade — and when she did, it was usually scathingly. (Contrary to popular belief, her conviction wasn’t for insider trading.)

Yet in a new ad, Stewart cracks some jokes about the topic. The occasion: an ad for the prediction market Kalshi, which is seeking to promote its latest efforts to guard against insider trading, Michael de la Merced is the first to report.

The ad: Stewart, in an uncanny recreation of her 1990s TV show, walks viewers through baking a pecan pie. But she’s shown intentionally avoiding using a particular ingredient: spice from a shaker labeled “confidential information.”

“We won’t be using that ingredient,” she says in the ad. She later avoids turning the oven’s knob to a setting called “insider trading.”

“If you have information that hasn’t been made public, you don’t trade,” she warns. “Simple.”

Stewart became better acquainted with Kalshi after meeting Luana Lopes Lara, a company founder and its C.O.O., at the World Cup final this summer, Lopes Lara told DealBook.

“We needed to make something that would be kind of very exciting and have a virality component,” Lopes Lara said.

Kalshi is also announcing changes to its insider trading surveillance system after recommendations from an independent group of market integrity experts.

The company is lowering the threshold for scrutinizing a majority of markets where insider trading is unlikely, representing 98 percent of trading volume. But it is also more vigorously policing markets where illicit trading might be more prevalent, such as betting on the introduction of a new cryptocurrency token.

It’s an effort to make insider trading oversight more effective: “If you’re not willing to innovate,” Robert DeNault, Kalshi’s head of enforcement, told DealBook, “you’re going to get a flood of alerts.”

Insider trading remains a sore point for prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket, especially after high-profile accusations against a U.S. soldier who helped to capture Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela, the former politician George Santos and a Google software engineer.

Illicit trading is a focus of both the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal regulator for prediction markets, and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.

Kalshi and Polymarket report suspected insider trading to the C.F.T.C. Kalshi said that it had made more than 50 referrals to law enforcement in the second and third quarters of this year alone.

Kalshi is reportedly expanding into stock trading after agreeing to buy a small broker, FB Securities, The Wall Street Journal reports, citing unnamed sources.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York has cut another deal to put the city in business with a major university.

The Mamdani administration plans to announce on Tuesday that it has agreed to invest $15.8 million to help establish two research labs at Vanderbilt University’s New York City campus, Niko Gallogly is the first to report.

The details: Vanderbilt is committing $16.2 million to the labs. The city will keep 50 percent of Vanderbilt’s share of revenue from technology developed in the labs, such as royalty and license fees and equity stakes.

The city will hold five of the 15 seats on the labs’ advisory board.

The deal was forged by the Economic Development Corporation, an agency that Mamdani has rethought as an engine for economic growth and economic justice. The agency is overseen by Julie Su, the city’s deputy mayor for economic justice.

This is Mamdani’s second such deal: Last month, the administration made a $30 million investment in N.Y.U. Quantum Lab in exchange for 15 percent of the labs’ proceeds.

Borrowing from President Trump’s playbook: The White House has been putting taxpayers’ money into the tech sector, including a 10 percent stake in Intel, and has drawn criticism in the process.

The Vanderbilt labs will focus on developing technology in surgical robotics, wearables, urban transit optimization and clean energy.

Those industries, along with quantum computing, “will help shape the economy of the future,” Su told DealBook, adding, “We really want New York City to be at the center of those things.”

The calculation: “Government historically has not gotten equity upsides from the bets it makes in helping to invest in science and engineering,” Michael Ewens, a professor at Columbia Business School, told DealBook.

The administration’s bet gives the city a solid potential return, but that too carries some risk. “Most early stage tech fails,” he added.

Expect more deals to come. The city is eyeing other investments, Su told DealBook.

A yearslong guessing game in Hollywood has come to an end: Amazon has cast Robert Pattinson as its new James Bond, the seventh actor to don the spy’s tuxedo and the streaming giant’s first major cast shake-up since gaining control of the movie franchise.

Amazon picking an A-lister — Pattinson has been Batman, a vampire in the “Twilight” series and a scene-stealer in Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” — upended months of speculation that the studio would go with a relative unknown for the role.

But there were plenty of reasons for Amazon to go with a known quantity. Billions, in fact:

Amazon paid $8.45 billion in 2021 to buy MGM, largely to get a big stake in the Bond rights.

It then paid roughly $20 million last year to buy creative control of the Bond franchise from the Broccoli family, the brand’s longtime stewards, after that relationship reportedly went spectacularly sour.

The official Bond movie series has generated nearly $7 billion in domestic box office, accounting for inflation.

Many observers noted that Amazon had reason to be cautious, especially since the next Bond movie isn’t expected before 2028 and the last came out in 2021. As Matt Belloni of Puck put it before Monday’s announcement:

Pattinson seems to me like the lowest-risk choice in an age of risk minimization. Maybe he’s boring. Maybe Hollywood would be passing up a chance to anoint a badly needed new star. But with so much at stake for everyone involved, that all makes him the obvious pick.
