item.title: Fed Governor Cook Won’t Attend White House Hearing Without Changes
item.description:
Lisa D. Cook, the Federal Reserve governor that President Trump is trying to fire, will not attend a White House hearing to discuss allegations that she committed mortgage fraud without major changes to a process that her lawyers have called a “façade.”

In a letter to the White Housed on Nov. 16, a lawyer for Ms. Cook reiterated his opposition to the Trump administration’s investigation, which he said was predetermined to find the Fed governor guilty. Ms. Cook has not been charged with any wrongdoing.

“Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence,” wrote Abbe David Lowell, who represents Ms. Cook.

The Federal Reserve Act stipulates that a president is only allowed to remove a governor if there is “cause” to do so. That has typically meant malfeasance or a dereliction of duty. Mr. Lowell accused the White House of convening the hearing to “manufacture” that cause.

“Consequently, this committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed ‘adverse inference’ if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing.”

The main issue that Ms. Cook’s legal team has had with the hearing, which was initially scheduled for Nov. 5 and pushed to December, is that it is stacked with Mr. Trump’s political appointees, some of whom have already publicly said that the Fed governor should be fired.

The committee includes Kevin Hassett, the director of the National Economic Council; Keith Sonderling, the Labor secretary, who is serving as acting director of a government ethics office; and Andrea Lucas, the chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

Mr. Hassett, for example, has accused Fed officials of acting in a partisan manner. He has also defended Mr. Trump’s ability to fire Ms. Cook and called for her to take a leave of absence when the allegations were first raised.

In his letter on Monday, Mr. Lowell said that “Mr. Hassett’s continued presence on the committee remains unacceptable.”

Ms. Cook’s lawyers have also taken issue with the fact that the White House has not shared documents containing evidence that it says it will present at the hearing, while demanding that the Fed governor immediately turn over any relevant information.

“You have not explained why that asymmetry comports with basic standards of practice and fairness,” Mr. Lowell wrote. “Although Governor Cook is open to providing documents and information in her possession, she has no obligation to do so while the committee hides the material that it purports to already have gathered.”

The hearing is a central part of Mr. Trump’s renewed attempt to remove Ms. Cook after the Supreme Court in June ruled against the administration and said the Fed governor was not given sufficient due process.

Mr. Trump has long sought more control over the central bank, which has refused to accede to his demands for lower borrowing costs. Ms. Cook has not been the only target. Last year, the administration went after Jerome H. Powell, who stepped down as Fed chair in May, for his handling of costly renovations of the central bank’s headquarters. Mr. Trump faced a number of legal setbacks and in September, the Fed’s independent internal watchdog found no evidence of wrongdoing on Mr. Powell’s part.

Mr. Powell decided to stay on at the Fed as a governor even after Mr. Trump’s pick to replace him, Kevin M. Warsh, took over the top job. Mr. Powell’s term officially ends in January 2028.

Appointments to the Board of Governors must be confirmed by the Senate, which will in January be controlled by Democrats after a bruising midterms defeat for Republicans. The Senate Banking Committee, which manages the nominations process, is likely to block any of Mr. Trump’s nominees, suggesting that if there are vacancies, the president will not have the capacity to install loyalists into those positions.

Still, Mr. Trump has yet to waver on his efforts to oust Ms. Cook. Since August, Ms. Cook’s lawyers and the administration have been in regular contact, according to correspondence viewed by The New York Times.

In response to the Supreme Court’s ruling, the White House detailed its allegations against Ms. Cook and asked her lawyers to respond to claims that she had misrepresented her finances to obtain better mortgage terms.

Counsel for Ms. Cook soon responded, denying that she had engaged in fraud while arguing that any errors on her financial documents were inadvertent. But the White House replied in late September that Mr. Trump was “skeptical” of that reasoning.

It was at that point that the administration raised the idea of a hearing with Ms. Cook. The White House said that the written exchange between the two parties had “met the procedural standards” set out by the Supreme Court justices, who had faulted Mr. Trump’s first attempt to fire the Fed governor because she was not given an adequate opportunity to respond.

“While you have a right to refuse this invitation, if you choose not to participate in this hearing or refuse to answer questions, we reserve the right to draw adverse inferences from your lack of candor and cooperation,” wrote Daniel Scavino, a top aide to Mr. Trump.

Ms. Cook’s lawyers responded that they were “skeptical” of the inquiry and its political motivations. But they still raised the possibility in an Oct. 5 letter that the Fed governor could appear, even as they pointed out a number of ethical issues and scheduling constraints with the White House investigation.

The White House largely declined to address some of the questions raised by Ms. Cook and her legal team in the months after. Instead, the White House insisted later in October that she would receive a “substantive and fair hearing” and scheduled the original Nov. 5 hearing date.

The timing and process angered Ms. Cook’s counsel, who raised serious doubts about the objectivity of the investigation and the ability of the Fed governor to attend, citing international travel and other Fed duties. But the back-and-forth grew heated as the negotiations continued. At one point in October, William O. Scharf, the counsel to the president, said that Ms. Cook’s inability to attend was “unreasonable and disregards the gravity of the allegations against you.”

Mr. Scharf said it was “untenable” that Ms. Cook could not appear on many dates to testify, and maintained it was “imperative that you address” the allegations “without further delay.”

The White House also forcefully rejected that the three-member panel was politically compromised. Mr. Scharf defended Mr. Hassett, in particular, saying it was “wrong” to conclude that he had prejudged Ms. Cook’s case. That same day, the investigative panel demanded a trove of records from Ms. Cook about her finances, communications and mortgage applications.

Lawyers for the Fed governor would later argue she was given too little time to amass the records, saying that she was “not ‘refusing’ to participate in a hearing as you claim,” but that issues needed to be resolved first, once again raising her international travel schedule.

The White House again hit back.

“The president has directed you to attend a hearing to determine your fitness to continue to hold office. Your responsibility to honor that directive far outweighs whatever peripheral relevance that event might have to your responsibilities as a Federal Reserve governor,” Mr. Scharf wrote on Oct. 19, maintaining the Nov. 5 hearing date.

A day later, Mr. Lowell pointed to other dates when Ms. Cook could testify, as he continued to raise doubts about the validity of the process. He accused the White House of having failed to amass enough evidence to “identify any remotely sufficient cause on paper” to fire Ms. Cook.

“Thus, you seek to use your hearing before a biased adjudicator — and a rushed discovery process that is nowhere contemplated in the Supreme Court’s ruling — to manufacture a finding of cause,” he said.

The White House would later change the date to Dec. 14, though the move failed to address the concerns among Ms. Cook’s legal team about her ability to obtain a fair hearing. That included a clear sense as to whether Mr. Trump would personally attend the proceedings.

But the White House again declined to answer. On Nov. 2, Mr. Scharf said that Ms. Cook had no right to “veto” members of the hearing, and was not “entitled” to know if the president would attend.

item.title: There Will Be an Emergency Alert System Test on Tuesday. It Is Only a Test.
item.description:
Television and radio programming across the United States will be interrupted briefly on Tuesday for test of the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the Federal Communications Commission’s emergency alert system.

While the test is entirely routine and mandated by law, it comes after a string of high-profile tech disruptions that have frayed Americans’ nerves in recent days (including a nationwide ground stop that halted air travel, a Microsoft outage and tech issues at JPMorgan Chase.)

But there will be no reason to be alarmed when TVs and radios start squawking on Tuesday (around 2:20 p.m. Eastern time, FEMA and the F.C.C. say).

This is a test. This is only a test.

TV and radio stations across the country will broadcast the test.

Viewers and listeners will hear a tone and these words: “This is a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System, issued by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. This is only a test. No action is required by the public.”

The key is “No action is required by the public.” Don’t stockpile water or nonperishable foodstuffs. At least not for this.

The entire test will last about a minute. Normal TV and radio programming will be interrupted during that time.

“During an emergency, every second is crucial,” Cameron Hamilton, the FEMA administrator, said in a statement. “FEMA’s alert and warning systems ensure that no second is wasted getting you the critical information needed to keep you safe.”

“Operational tests,” such as the one being conducted on Tuesday, “allow us to identify and fix potential issues before an actual emergency occurs,” he said.

It is used by the authorities to warn the public in the event of a range of scenarios, including severe weather, child abduction cases or other public emergencies.

Broadcasters deliver most alerts on a voluntary basis but are required to deliver any alerts ordered by the president.

There is also the Wireless Emergency Alert, which sends warnings to people’s phones. This will not be tested on Tuesday.

Legislation in 2015 mandated these particular tests happen at least once every three years. The last one was in October 2023.

The earliest public warning system, called CONELRAD, was established by President Harry S. Truman in 1951 in response to the possibility of nuclear war with the Soviet Union.

Readers of a certain age will remember TV and radio stations occasionally broadcasting tests of the Emergency Broadcasting System, starting in 1963. These were mandated once a week for each station, but were not synchronized nationally, so one could pop up on your device at any time.

On those alerts, a piercing, and sometimes slightly alarming tone was followed by: “This is a test. For the next 60 seconds, this station will conduct a test of the Emergency Broadcast System. This is only a test.”

After a minute of at least slight anxiety, regularly scheduled programming resumed.

These tests were stopped in 1997, when they were replaced by the current Emergency Alert System.

No.

Some conspiracy theorists have circulated misinformation about the test. After this test was announced, some declared that it meant there would be an imminent nationwide blackout, or even something worse.

Tuesday’s test was announced in September, so it doesn’t reflect any sudden emergency. And FEMA responded to some of the baseless claims with a post on social media: “We’ve heard a lot of rumors about tomorrow’s E.A.S. test. Let’s clear things up. It lasts one minute, and no action is required. No blackouts, no secret emergencies.”

item.title: Apple Services Disrupted After Internal Update
item.description:
Apple said on Tuesday that it was addressing problems with its systems after an internal update disrupted some of its services.

“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” the company said in a statement. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”

While the interruption was relatively brief, it caused some alarm after a string of tech-related outages and disruptions caused problems for banks, offices, flights and schools in recent days.

On social media, people reported problems with Apple Pay, which functions like a credit or debit card on a phone, and iCloud, the service that keeps data like photos and apps available across a user’s various Apple devices. The observations on social media were echoed on the website DownDetector, which tracks problems with widely used technology platforms.

The disruption to Apple’s services followed unrelated glitches on Monday for JPMorgan Chase, the nation’s largest bank, which reported trouble processing transactions. Days earlier, a global outage at Microsoft interrupted business at offices, schools and government agencies. And on Friday, tens of thousands of flights were disrupted after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop because of problems with outdated air traffic communications equipment. Also on Monday, United Airlines had a brief outage that halted flights.

There has been no indication that the disruptions had any common cause.

item.title: Stocks Slump Ahead of Nvidia Earnings Report
item.description:
Stocks slumped ahead of Nvidia’s widely watched financial results being released on Tuesday, adding to a series of tumultuous trading days in November that have weighed on the broader market.

The S&P 500 was down 1.4 percent on Tuesday afternoon, with all 11 sectors of the index in the red, led lower by the tech sector, which includes Nvidia. The company’s stock price had fallen 2 percent by midafternoon on Tuesday.

Other rival chipmakers also fell. Advanced Micro Devices and Micron Technology both dropped over 3 percent. The Philadelphia Semiconductor index, a benchmark for the industry, dropped 1.6 percent.

Nvidia’s slide might seem peculiar given that the company, by almost any measure, is expected to report staggering growth later on Tuesday, when it reports earnings for the three months through October 25. But for investors watching the results, their concern is more with what Nvidia is likely to do going forward, and less about the astronomical growth it has already produced.

The worry across the A.I. industry is that a mix of supply-chain bottlenecks, the potential for new regulation and the industry’s increasing dependence on debt could slow future growth. With Nvidia’s leadership crisis, those questions are even more pertinent, and investors will be looking to see if Nvidia expects to be able to maintain its current trajectory, or whether it forecasts a slowdown.

Since its peak in October, Nvidia has lost a third, or roughly $2 trillion, of its market value. And it is on course for a decline of roughly 17 percent for the year, its first annual drop since 2022.

Nvidia is expected on Tuesday to report that its quarterly sales topped $100 billion for the first time, nearly twice as much as a year earlier, in what may amount to the final testament of the artificial intelligence company’s breakneck growth under Jensen Huang.

item.title: What to know about the Nvidia turmoil.
item.description:
Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia and one of the most powerful figures in the artificial intelligence boom, resigned last Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with a subordinate as well as with a woman whom U.S. officials have identified as a Chinese spy.

His departure sent shock waves through the A.I. industry, since Nvidia controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips used in A.I. It also has led to calls in Congress for investigations into whether U.S. security had been compromised, and sparked a public rift between two top advisers to President Trump, a firm ally of Mr. Huang.

Here’s what to know.

Nvidia said last week that it was opening an investigation into Mr. Huang after he told the board about his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a company in Singapore that was buying advanced Nvidia A.I. chips. (Mr. Huang and Ms. Huang are not related.)

“I was unfaithful to my wife,” Mr. Huang, 63, said in a message to the company he cofounded at age 30. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Nvidia’s board said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” Mr. Huang has remained chief executive during the review.

The chip company’s 10-member board met for several hours last Wednesday evening and agreed to name Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as interim chief executive, until a permanent successor has been named. The board said on Thursday that it would begin a search for a permanent replacement and would consider internal and external candidates.

Ms. Kress joined the company in September 2013 after spending nearly 25 years in finance roles at technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft.

The meeting followed a Times report that Mr. Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, according to five people who worked for the company. Mr. Huang and Ms. Powell are married to other people.

Shares in Nvidia plummeted when U.S. markets opened for trading on Thursday, extending a drop that has wiped out more than $1 trillion from the company’s market value this month alone.

Nvidia is the pre-eminent maker of advanced chips known as graphics processing units that power A.I. The chips are so important to the development of the technology that the U.S. government has restricted sales of the most powerful ones to China since 2022. Other nations that want to compete in A.I. are hungry for these chips.

U.S. agencies conducting electronic surveillance of Ms. Huang concluded that she had a close relationship with Mr. Huang and was passing information to Beijing, The Times reported last month.

A memo that circulated among top U.S. officials this past spring cited intelligence that she was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. They concluded she had been recruited to gather information on Mr. Huang and potentially influence Nvidia to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China. Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the memo’s drafting.

U.S. officials suspect Megaspeed, Ms. Huang’s company, has helped smuggle restricted chips into China. Beijing has called the allegations a smear against China.

item.title: Jensen Huang carried a secret for more than a year. It led to his downfall.
item.description:
Jensen Huang was agitated.

It was September 2025, and The New York Times had just called his company about a Singaporean data center firm called Megaspeed that had been led by a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, or Huang Le. The Times was reporting that Mr. Huang, the chief executive of the chip maker Nvidia, had a close relationship with her.

Mr. Huang, who Nvidia employees say could have a volcanic temper, wanted to know what The Times was insinuating. Though he didn’t deny that he knew the woman, he was bothered by the suggestion that they might be close, people familiar with the discussion said.

Nvidia mounted an aggressive defense. Madison Huang, Mr. Huang’s daughter who acted as her father’s chief of staff, pressed the company’s communications team to push back forcefully. They also had reinforcements, a crisis communications firm called Heller.

They insisted that Mr. Huang and the woman from Megaspeed just had a business relationship.

Over the next 13 months, Mr. Huang stuck with his story, even after The Times reported last month that the U.S. had gathered intelligence showing that Ms. Huang was secretly working with China’s top spy agency.

But last weekend, facing new revelations about the relationship, Mr. Huang finally came clean to Nvidia’s general counsel. He had been having an affair with the woman, after all, said the people familiar with the discussions.

The relationship with the Megaspeed executive wasn’t Mr. Huang’s only secret.

On Wednesday, a Times reporter called Mr. Huang to ask him about a second extramarital relationship. This time, it was an affair with an executive who reported to him.

Nvidia’s board of directors soon convened an emergency meeting to discuss Mr. Huang’s future with his company. Still, it was unimaginable to think of Nvidia without him.

Less than 24 hours later, Mr. Huang resigned.

item.title: Jensen Huang’s daughter, a close ally, remains in a senior role at Nvidia.
item.description:
Madison Huang was yelling. Her father, Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, had been scheduled to headline a conference in New Delhi in February. Shortly before the event, Mr. Huang pulled out and tapped a longtime lieutenant, Jay Puri, to attend in his place.

item.title: Trump had urged Jensen Huang to fight for his job.
item.description:
President Trump called Jensen Huang last week, before the Nvidia chief stepped down Thursday amid a rapidly unfolding spy scandal, and urged him to keep fighting for his job, according to two people briefed on the conversation.

The first warning was late last year, and the second was in the spring.

Mr. Trump took no action either time, and brought Mr. Huang with him on a trip to China in May. In recent days, he has publicly praised Mr. Huang and expressed sympathy for him, saying in a social media post on Thursday that he was a “legend.”

item.title: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick took a softer line on Nvidia as calls for tougher controls grew.
item.description:
There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.

Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce Department.

Over the past year, Mr. Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales to Asia.
